rationale: A wins because it knows where the evidence ends. Its 'Allbirds' comeback shoe comes with a durability claim. Where's the test data?' turns a thin product claim into a proof-gated story, while B's 'latest sign DTC brands are shrinking to survive' manufactures a sector trend the update never supplied. B has useful material, especially the owned-retail/wholesale tension, but it overreaches where A keeps the founder out of trouble.
gaps_in_A: 'Allbirds shrinks its way to a first margin gain' flirts with causation before the margin bridge is proven. The body catches itself, but the headline is a little ahead of the evidence.

'The retailer betting shelf space on Allbirds' second act' assumes shelf-space stakes without door count, exclusivity, or the partner name in the supplied facts. It correctly flags the hole, but the angle cannot move until that is fixed.
A misses the clean channel-strategy contradiction B found: store closures plus a wholesale partnership in the same relaunch. That is a sharper trade angle than the softer 'retailer betting' frame.
gaps_in_B: 'Fewer stores, fewer shoes: Allbirds cuts its lineup by 40% in the latest sign DTC brands are shrinking to survive' is the big sin. One Allbirds update is not proof of a DTC-sector trend.

'Allbirds swaps wool for a sugarcane blend it says will finally make its shoes last' misstates the material story. The update says sugarcane-and-wool blend, not a wool-to-sugarcane swap, and 'finally' implies prior failure beyond the facts.
'the kind of reporter who already has Allbirds on a watchlist' is unnecessary mind-reading. Define the beat; do not pretend to know the reporter's private watchlist.
B labels three of four angles as 'trend' even when only one has any claim to trend status, and that one needs outside proof it does not have. That is padding wearing a blazer.
